raw_text:
Unit 1: Introduction to the Constitution of India

Learning Objectives

By the end of this unit, learners will be able to:

   1. Describe the historical background that led to the framing of the Indian Constitution.

   2. Explain the significance of the Objectives Resolution and the debates in the
      Constituent Assembly.

   3. Identify and interpret the key features of the Indian Constitution.

   4. Analyze the structure of the Constitution, including the Preamble, Parts, and
      Schedules.

   5. Evaluate how constitutional amendments have shaped the evolution of the
      Constitution.

   6. Discuss the foundational principles underlying the Indian Constitution.

   7. Demonstrate an understanding of the intent and vision of the Constitution makers.

Structure:

1.1 Overview of the Historical Background Leading to the Framing of the Indian Constitution

1.2 Objectives Resolution and Constituent Assembly Debates

1.3 Key Features of the Constitution: Preamble, Parts, and Schedules

1.4 Evolution of the Constitution Through Amendments

1.5 Summary

1.6 Keywords

1.7 Self-Assessment Questions

1.8 References

1.1 Overview of the Historical Background Leading to the Framing of the Indian Constitution

The Constitution of India, adopted in 1950, did not emerge in a vacuum. It was the result of a
long historical process influenced by colonial governance, the freedom struggle, and the socio-
political evolution of Indian society. The journey toward framing a democratic constitution
began with early British laws and reforms, gained momentum through sustained nationalist
demands for self-rule, and culminated in the establishment of a Constituent Assembly. Each
of these phases contributed crucially to shaping the ideas, principles, and values embedded
in the Indian Constitution.

1.1.1 Colonial Legacy and Indian Governance Before 1947

• Regulating Act of 1773

   •   The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first significant attempt by the British Parliament
       to control and supervise the affairs of the East India Company in India.

   •   It marked the beginning of constitutional development in British India and laid the
       foundation of central administration.

   •   Key features:

           o   Establishment of a Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings was the first).

           o   A council of four members was created to assist the Governor-General in
               administrative decisions.

           o   The Act made the Governor of Bombay and Madras subordinate to the
               Governor-General of Bengal.

           o   It created a Supreme Court at Calcutta in 1774 with jurisdiction over British
               subjects.

   •   Importance:

           o   Introduced centralized administration.

           o   Highlighted the necessity of legislative and judicial reforms.

• Government of India Act, 1858

   •   This Act was enacted after the Revolt of 1857, leading to the end of the rule of the East
       India Company.

   •   Major provisions:

           o   The British Crown took over the administration of India.

          o   A Secretary of State for India was appointed with complete authority, assisted
              by a council.

          o   The Governor-General was designated as the Viceroy of India, acting as the
              representative of the British Crown.

   •   Significance:

          o   Initiated direct rule by the British Crown.

          o   Centralized administration and brought greater control from London.

• Government of India Act, 1919

   •   Also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.

   •   Introduced diarchy in the provinces:

          o   Transferred subjects (administered by Indian ministers): education, public
              health, agriculture.

          o   Reserved subjects (retained by British officials): law and order, finance.

   •   Established a bicameral legislature at the center.

   •   Expanded legislative councils and gave more Indians participation in governance.

   •   Importance:

          o   First attempt at decentralizing powers to Indians.

          o   Exposed limitations and dissatisfaction, paving the way for further demands.

• Government of India Act, 1935

   •   Considered the most comprehensive British law on Indian governance.

   •   Major features:

          o   Introduced provincial autonomy by abolishing diarchy at the provincial level.

          o   Proposed an all-India Federation with princely states and British Indian
              provinces.

          o   Created a bicameral legislature at the center (though not implemented fully).

          o   Introduced the concept of a Federal Court.

   •   Significance:

          o   Served as a blueprint for the Indian Constitution.

          o   Several features, including federalism and emergency powers, were later
              adopted in independent India.

• British Influence on Indian Legal-Administrative Systems

   •   Introduction of codified laws: Indian Penal Code (1860), Civil Procedure Code, Criminal
       Procedure Code, etc.

   •   Evolution of an organized judiciary based on British common law.

   •   Development of a civil services system to manage bureaucracy (later Indian Civil
       Services).

   •   British emphasis on centralized control and law and order shaped the administrative
       framework.

1.1.2 Indian Freedom Struggle and Constitutional Demand

• Role of Indian National Congress

   •   Founded in 1885, the Indian National Congress (INC) became the primary political
       platform advocating for Indian self-rule.

   •   Initial phases involved petitions and resolutions for more Indian representation in
       legislative councils.

   •   Over time, especially after 1905, the INC evolved into a mass movement demanding
       Swaraj (self-rule).

   •   After World War I, the INC began demanding Purna Swaraj (complete independence)
       in 1929.

   •   The party began pressing for a constitution made by Indians, not dictated by colonial
       powers.

• Nehru Report (1928) and Simon Commission

   •   Simon Commission (1927):

          o   Formed by the British without any Indian member.

          o   Faced widespread boycott and protests across India.

          o   Its exclusion of Indian voices spurred nationalist leaders to propose their own
              constitutional framework.

   •   Nehru Report (1928):

          o   Drafted by a committee chaired by Motilal Nehru.

          o   First Indian attempt at framing a constitution.

          o   Proposed:

                   ▪   Dominion status for India.

                   ▪   Fundamental rights.

                   ▪   Universal adult franchise.

                   ▪   Federal structure.

          o   Although it did not lead to immediate changes, it represented growing
              constitutional awareness among Indians.

• Round Table Conferences and the Demand for a Constituent Assembly

   •   Held in London in three phases between 1930 and 1932.

   •   Aimed at discussing future governance of India.

   •   Major Indian parties like the Congress initially boycotted the first conference but
       participated in later ones.

   •   Outcomes:

          o   Differences on communal representation and federal structure remained
              unresolved.

          o   British leaders acknowledged the inevitability of constitutional change.

   •   Demand for a Constituent Assembly emerged strongly:

          o   Popularized by the INC and supported by other nationalists.

          o   The idea was to have Indians frame their own Constitution, rather than one
              imposed by the British Parliament.

          o   Became a central demand during the Quit India Movement and later
              negotiations.

1.1.3 Establishment of the Constituent Assembly

• Cabinet Mission Plan

   •   Announced in 1946 by the British government.

   •   Proposed the formation of a Constituent Assembly to draft the Constitution of India.

   •   Key recommendations:

          o   A union of India with both British provinces and princely states.

          o   Grouping of provinces with autonomy.

          o   A Constituent Assembly with 389 members to be elected by the provincial
              assemblies.

   •   The plan was accepted by the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League,
       though differences soon emerged.

• Election and Composition of the Assembly

   •   Elections to the Constituent Assembly were held in July 1946.

   •   Composition:

          o   Total of 389 members.

          o   292 from British provinces.

          o   93 from princely states.

          o   4 from chief commissioner’s provinces.

   •   After the partition in 1947, the total strength came down to 299.

   •   Representation:

          o   Members were elected indirectly by provincial legislatures.

          o   Included lawyers, social workers, intellectuals, and political leaders.

          o   Diverse ideologies and regional representations were present.

• Role of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar

   •   Appointed as the Chairman of the Drafting Committee.

   •   Played a pivotal role in:

          o   Structuring the legal and institutional framework of the Constitution.

          o   Integrating ideas from various sources, including Western democracies and
              Indian traditions.

          o   Advocating for social justice, fundamental rights, and the abolition of
              untouchability.

   •   Recognized as the chief architect of the Indian Constitution.

   •   Known for balancing federalism, parliamentary democracy, and individual rights.

1.2 Objectives Resolution and Constituent Assembly Debates

The Objectives Resolution and the Constituent Assembly Debates played a crucial role in laying
the philosophical and structural foundations of the Indian Constitution. The Objectives
Resolution, introduced in 1946, expressed the vision and aspirations of the Indian people for
a sovereign, democratic, and just state. The debates in the Constituent Assembly, spanning
nearly three years, provided a forum for discussing and deciding upon the core features of the
Constitution. Together, they shaped the direction of constitutional development in India.

1.2.1 Objectives Resolution

• Date and Proposer (Jawaharlal Nehru)

   •   The Objectives Resolution was introduced by Jawaharlal Nehru in the Constituent
       Assembly on 13 December 1946.

   •   It was moved just a few days after the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly, which
       convened on 9 December 1946.

   •   The Resolution was adopted unanimously by the Assembly on 22 January 1947.

   •   Nehru, as the leader of the Indian National Congress and a central figure in the
       freedom struggle, was entrusted with this responsibility.

   •   The introduction of the Resolution was a seminal moment, representing the first
       articulation of the core values the Constitution would later embody.

   •   It served as a guiding light for the Constituent Assembly during the drafting of various
       constitutional provisions.

• Core Principles Stated in the Resolution

   •   The Objectives Resolution laid down the fundamental principles that were to guide the
       framing of the Constitution.

   •   Key principles included:

           o   India shall be an independent, sovereign republic.

           o   All power and authority of the sovereign, independent India, its constituent
               parts and organs of government, are derived from the people.

           o   The Constitution shall guarantee and secure to all the people of India:

                  ▪   Justice—social, economic, and political;

                  ▪   Equality of status and opportunity;

                  ▪   Freedom of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship, vocation,
                      association, and action.

          o   Adequate safeguards shall be provided for minorities, backward and tribal
              areas, and depressed and other backward classes.

          o   The Constitution shall promote international peace and security.

          o   India shall be a federation.

   •   The Resolution emphasized unity in diversity, representative democracy, and the
       dignity of the individual.

• Influence on the Preamble

   •   The Preamble of the Constitution, adopted in 1949, closely reflects the language and
       spirit of the Objectives Resolution.

   •   Elements like sovereignty, justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity were directly
       derived from the Resolution.

   •   The phrase “We, the people of India…” embodies the democratic and popular
       sovereignty concept declared in the Resolution.

   •   The Resolution laid the ethical and political groundwork, influencing not only the
       Preamble but also the Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, and the structure of
       governance.

   •   It gave coherence and purpose to the drafting process, ensuring that the Constitution
       would reflect the will and aspirations of the Indian people.

1.2.2 Constituent Assembly Debates

• Duration and Major Sessions

   •   The Constituent Assembly met for the first time on 9 December 1946 and continued
       until the adoption of the Constitution on 26 November 1949.

   •   The Assembly held 11 sessions, spread over 165 days of debate.

   •   These sessions were:

          1. First Session – December 1946

          2. Second Session – January 1947

          3. Third Session – April–May 1947

           4. Fourth Session – July 1947

           5. Fifth Session – August 1947

           6. Sixth Session – January 1948

           7. Seventh Session – November 1948

           8. Eighth Session – May 1949

           9. Ninth Session – September 1949

           10. Tenth Session – October 1949

           11. Eleventh Session – November 1949

   •   The final session ended with the signing of the Constitution, which came into effect on
       26 January 1950.

• Key Issues Debated (e.g., Federal Structure, Language, Minority Rights)

   •   The Constituent Assembly debated a vast range of constitutional, legal, and
       philosophical issues.

   •   Some of the most significant debates included:

Federal Structure:

           o   There was a divide over whether India should have a unitary or federal system.

           o   The decision leaned toward a federal structure with a strong center, especially
               considering the challenges of post-partition India.

           o   Dr. Ambedkar justified a strong central authority due to the fear of regionalism
               and secessionism.

Official Language:

           o   One of the most contentious debates involved the choice of official language.

           o   There were competing claims for Hindi and English, with opposition from
               South Indian states for imposing Hindi.

           o   Eventually, Hindi in Devanagari script was adopted as the official language,
               with English to continue for a transitional period.

Minority Rights and Religious Freedom:

           o   The Assembly debated safeguards for religious, linguistic, and cultural
               minorities.

          o   There were differing opinions on separate electorates, reservations, and the
              protection of cultural identities.

          o   A decision was taken to provide affirmative action and cultural rights, but
              reject separate electorates.

Directive Principles and Fundamental Rights:

          o   Philosophical debates occurred over socio-economic rights vs civil-political
              rights.

          o   Eventually, Directive Principles were made non-justiciable, while Fundamental
              Rights were enforceable by courts.

Emergency Provisions:

          o   Emergency powers were discussed in detail due to fears of misuse.

          o   However, considering the tumultuous situation of the late 1940s, emergency
              provisions were incorporated with safeguards.

Structure of Government:

          o   The choice between presidential and parliamentary system was debated.

          o   The Assembly opted for the Westminster-style parliamentary system.

• Role of Prominent Members (e.g., Sardar Patel, Rajendra Prasad, etc.)

   •   Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (Chairman of the Drafting Committee):

          o   Provided the legal and structural framework of the Constitution.

          o   Advocated for liberty, equality, and fraternity as central principles.

   •   Jawaharlal Nehru (Head of the Union Constitution Committee):

          o   Introduced the Objectives Resolution.

          o   Played a crucial role in shaping foreign policy, economic principles, and
              democratic values.

   •   Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (Head of the Provincial Constitution Committee):

          o   Advocated for the integration of princely states.

          o   Played a key role in defining the federal structure and administrative setup.

   •   Rajendra Prasad (President of the Constituent Assembly):

          o   Ensured the smooth conduct of debates and upheld procedural fairness.

           o   His leadership maintained balance amidst ideological differences.

   •   Alladi Krishnaswamy Iyer and K.M. Munshi:

           o   Contributed significantly to the drafting and interpretation of legal provisions.

   •   T.T. Krishnamachari:

           o   Took over responsibilities during Ambedkar’s absence.

           o   Played a role in drafting financial provisions and government structure.

   •   Hansa Mehta, Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, and Durgabai Deshmukh:

           o   Advocated for gender justice, women’s rights, and social welfare provisions.

   •   The Assembly included members from different religions, regions, languages, and
       professions, ensuring inclusivity.

1.3 Key Features of the Constitution: Preamble, Parts, and Schedules

The Indian Constitution is the foundational legal document that establishes the structure,
functions, and principles of governance. Its key features are reflected through the Preamble,
the distinct Parts, and the Schedules. The Preamble outlines the Constitution's ideals and
objectives. The Parts organize substantive content into thematic areas such as rights, duties,
and the system of government. The Schedules add operational detail and administrative
clarity. Together, they provide a comprehensive legal and ideological framework that defines
the nature of the Indian state.

1.3.1 The Preamble

• Text and Significance

   •   The Preamble to the Indian Constitution reads as follows:

“WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN
SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens:

           o   JUSTICE, social, economic and political;

           o   LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship;

           o   EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all

           o   FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity
               of the Nation;

IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY
ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.”

   •   The Preamble serves as an introductory statement that reflects the philosophy,
       values, and objectives of the Constitution.

   •   It encapsulates the vision of the Constituent Assembly and acts as a guiding light for
       interpreting the Constitution.

   •   It declares India to be:

           o   Sovereign: India is independent in both internal and external affairs.

           o   Socialist: Commitment to social and economic equality.

           o   Secular: Equal treatment of all religions by the state.

           o   Democratic: Rule by elected representatives through universal adult franchise.

           o   Republic: Elected head of state and absence of monarchy.

   •   The values of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity form the core ideology of Indian
       democracy.

• Interpretation by Courts

   •   The Supreme Court of India has emphasized the importance of the Preamble in several
       landmark cases:

1. Berubari Union Case (1960):

           o   The Court held that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution.

           o   It could not be used for interpretation in case of ambiguity in constitutional
               provisions.

2. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973):

           o   The Supreme Court reversed the earlier view and held that the Preamble is a
               part of the Constitution.

           o   It plays a significant interpretative role, particularly in understanding the basic
               structure of the Constitution.

           o   The Court ruled that any amendment which alters the basic structure is invalid.

3. LIC of India v. Consumer Education and Research Centre (1995):

           o   Reiterated that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution and forms
               its identity.

           o   It reflects the goals and aspirations of the people.

   •   Courts have repeatedly used the Preamble to uphold constitutional morality, civil
       liberties, and judicial accountability.

• Impact of the 42nd Amendment

   •   The 42nd Amendment Act of 1976 made significant changes to the Preamble.

   •   Three words were inserted:

           o   “Socialist”

           o   “Secular”

           o   “Integrity”

   •   The amendment was carried out during the Emergency period under Prime Minister
       Indira Gandhi’s government.

   •   It emphasized the commitment of the state to planned economy and religious
       neutrality.

   •   The amendment was criticized for being passed during a period of limited political
       dissent but has been retained to reflect the spirit of inclusion and equality.

   •   The changes reaffirmed India's position as a modern welfare state and were later
       validated by courts as consistent with the basic structure doctrine.

1.3.2 Parts of the Constitution

• Total Number of Parts and Their Themes

   •   The Constitution is divided into 25 Parts (originally 22), each addressing a major
       functional or structural theme.

   •   As of the latest amendment, the Parts are as follows:

           o   Part I – The Union and its Territory

           o   Part II – Citizenship

           o   Part III – Fundamental Rights

           o   Part IV – Directive Principles of State Policy

           o   Part IVA – Fundamental Duties (added by 42nd Amendment)

          o   Part V – Union Government

          o   Part VI – State Government

          o   Part VII – (Repealed)

          o   Part VIII – Union Territories

          o   Part IX – Panchayats

          o   Part IXA – Municipalities

          o   Part IXB – Co-operative Societies

          o   Part X – Scheduled and Tribal Areas

          o   Part XI – Relations between the Union and States

          o   Part XII – Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits

          o   Part XIII – Trade, Commerce and Intercourse

          o   Part XIV – Services under the Union and States

          o   Part XIVA – Tribunals

          o   Part XV – Elections

          o   Part XVI – Special Provisions relating to certain classes

          o   Part XVII – Official Language

          o   Part XVIII – Emergency Provisions

          o   Part XIX – Miscellaneous

          o   Part XX – Amendment of the Constitution

          o   Part XXI – Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions

          o   Part XXII – Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative Text in Hindi

   •   Each Part consists of Articles, the total number of which has increased from 395 to
       over 450 due to amendments.

• Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

   •   Part III – Fundamental Rights:

          o   Articles 12 to 35.

          o   Include the right to equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, freedom
              of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies.

          o   Enforceable by courts; considered the heart and soul of the Constitution.

   •   Part IV – Directive Principles of State Policy:

          o   Articles 36 to 51.

          o   Lay down principles for governance, aiming at creating a welfare state.

          o   Not enforceable by courts but fundamental in governance.

          o   Include provision for adequate livelihood, equal pay, free legal aid, promotion
              of education, and environmental protection.

• Structure of Government: Union and State Relations

   •   Part V and Part VI:

          o   Define the Union (Central) and State Governments respectively.

          o   Specify roles of President, Prime Minister, Council of Ministers, Governor,
              Chief Minister, and State Councils.

   •   Part XI:

          o   Outlines the distribution of legislative and executive powers between the
              Union and States.

          o   Introduces the Union List, State List, and Concurrent List under the Seventh
              Schedule.

   •   The structure supports a quasi-federal system, with the center holding more power
       in critical areas such as national security and foreign policy.

1.3.3 Schedules of the Constitution

• Overview of 12 Schedules

   •   The Indian Constitution has 12 Schedules, each adding specificity and administrative
       detail to constitutional provisions.

   •   Brief overview:

          o   1st Schedule – Names of states and union territories; territorial jurisdiction.

          o   2nd Schedule – Salaries and allowances of officials including President,
              Governors, Judges, etc.

          o   3rd Schedule – Forms of oaths and affirmations.

           o   4th Schedule – Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats among states and union
               territories.

           o   5th Schedule – Administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled
               Tribes.

           o   6th Schedule – Provisions for administration of tribal areas in Assam,
               Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.

           o   7th Schedule – Distribution of powers between Union and State legislatures.

           o   8th Schedule – List of official languages (originally 14, now 22).

           o   9th Schedule – Laws protected from judicial review under Article 31B
               (originally for land reforms).

           o   10th Schedule – Provisions related to anti-defection (added by 52nd
               Amendment).

           o   11th Schedule – Powers and responsibilities of Panchayats (added by 73rd
               Amendment).

           o   12th Schedule – Powers and responsibilities of Municipalities (added by 74th
               Amendment).

• Significance of Select Schedules

   •   5th Schedule:

           o   Deals with governance of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.

           o   Provides for Tribes Advisory Councils and special governance structures.

           o   Aims to protect tribal autonomy and culture.

   •   6th Schedule:

           o   Provides for Autonomous District Councils in tribal areas of the Northeast.

           o   Ensures political and administrative autonomy.

           o   Significant for managing ethnic diversity and preventing alienation.

   •   8th Schedule:

           o   Lists 22 official languages recognized by the Constitution.

           o   Promotes linguistic diversity and language rights.

           o   Allows for inclusion of more languages through constitutional amendment.

   •   10th Schedule:

           o   Known as the Anti-Defection Law.

           o   Prevents elected legislators from switching parties after elections.

           o   Ensures political stability and accountability in parliamentary democracy.

1.4 Evolution of the Constitution Through Amendments

The Indian Constitution is a living document designed to evolve with time. To ensure its
adaptability, the Constitution provides a mechanism for amendments. Over the decades, the
Constitution has been amended multiple times to reflect changing political, social, and
economic needs. These amendments have helped address legal ambiguities, strengthen
democratic institutions, expand fundamental rights, and accommodate emerging governance
structures. The process of amendment is governed by Article 368, and several landmark
amendments, along with judicial interpretations, have significantly shaped the constitutional
framework.

1.4.1 Constitutional Amendment Process

• Article 368: Types of Amendments

   •   Article 368 of the Constitution of India lays down the procedure for amending the
       Constitution.

   •   It classifies amendments into three categories:

1. By Simple Majority of Parliament:

           o   These amendments are not considered amendments under Article 368.

           o   They can be passed like ordinary legislation.

           o   Examples include:

                  ▪   Admission or establishment of new states (Article 2, 3).

                  ▪   Formation of new states or alteration of areas, boundaries, or names of
                      existing states.

                  ▪   Changes in the Second, Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Schedules.

2. By Special Majority of Parliament:

           o   Requires a majority of the total membership of each House of Parliament.

           o   Also requires a two-thirds majority of the members present and voting.

           o   Most provisions of the Constitution are amended using this method.

           o   Examples include:

                   ▪   Amendment to Fundamental Rights.

                   ▪   Changes in the Directive Principles.

                   ▪   Changes to Union or State powers that do not affect federal structure.

3. By Special Majority of Parliament and Ratification by Half of the States:

           o   This is required when amendments affect the federal structure of the
               Constitution.

           o   In addition to a special majority in Parliament, at least half of the state
               legislatures must ratify the amendment.

           o   Examples include:

                   ▪   Election of the President.

                   ▪   Representation of states in Parliament.

                   ▪   Powers of the Union and State governments.

• Procedure for Amendment

   •   The amendment process under Article 368 includes the following steps:

1. Introduction of Bill:

           o   An amendment can be initiated only in Parliament.

           o   The bill can be introduced in either House: Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha.

           o   It does not require prior permission from the President.

2. Passage in Each House:

           o   The bill must be passed by a special majority:

                   ▪   A majority of the total membership of the House.

                   ▪   A two-thirds majority of the members present and voting.

           o   If both Houses pass the bill in the required manner, it proceeds to the next step.

3. Ratification by States (if required):

           o   For amendments affecting the federal structure, ratification by at least half of
               the state legislatures is necessary.

           o   No time limit is prescribed for obtaining state ratifications.

4. President’s Assent:

           o   After passing both Houses and obtaining state ratification (if applicable), the
               bill is sent to the President.

           o   The President is constitutionally bound to give assent and cannot return the
               bill.

   •   The amendment then becomes part of the Constitution and is formally added to the
       Constitution’s text.

1.4.2 Landmark Amendments

• 1st Amendment (1951)

   •   Context:

           o   Introduced to resolve judicial criticisms of government reforms and address
               certain limitations in the Fundamental Rights.

   •   Major changes:

           o   Added Article 31A and Article 31B to protect land reform laws from judicial
               review.

           o   Introduced the 9th Schedule to shelter laws from Fundamental Rights scrutiny.

           o   Amended Article 19 to impose reasonable restrictions on freedom of speech
               and expression.

   •   Impact:

           o   Asserted parliamentary supremacy in land redistribution.

           o   First example of curtailing Fundamental Rights for achieving socio-economic
               objectives.

• 42nd Amendment (1976)

   •   Known as the “Mini-Constitution” due to its extensive scope.

   •   Passed during the Emergency under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.

   •   Major provisions:

           o   Preamble amended: Added “Socialist,” “Secular,” and “Integrity.”

           o   Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) were added.

          o   Directive Principles given primacy over Fundamental Rights in case of conflict
              (Article 31C).

          o   Empowered Parliament to amend any part of the Constitution without judicial
              review.

          o   Weakened the judiciary by restricting its powers of review.

          o   Centralized authority by strengthening the Union government vis-à-vis States.

   •   Criticism:

          o   Passed under authoritarian conditions.

          o   Viewed as an attempt to curb democratic institutions.

• 44th Amendment (1978)

   •   Introduced by the Janata Party government post-Emergency.

   •   Aimed to restore democratic balance disturbed by the 42nd Amendment.

   •   Key changes:

          o   Article 352: Made it more difficult to declare Emergency; required written
              advice of the Cabinet.

          o   Article 19 and Article 21 were restored; Right to life and liberty made non-
              suspendable even during Emergency.

          o   Property rights were removed from Fundamental Rights and made a legal right
              under Article 300A.

          o   Curb on misuse of preventive detention.

   •   Reestablished constitutional safeguards and emphasized civil liberties.

• 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992)

   •   Landmark amendments that introduced local self-governance in rural and urban
       areas.

   •   73rd Amendment:

          o   Added Part IX and 11th Schedule.

          o   Provided constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs).

          o   Mandatory elections every 5 years.

          o   Reservation of seats for SCs, STs, and women.

          o     State Finance Commissions and Election Commissions were established.

   •   74th Amendment:

          o     Added Part IXA and 12th Schedule.

          o     Recognized Municipalities as institutions of urban local self-government.

          o     Defined three types: Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils, Nagar
                Panchayats.

          o     Assigned functional responsibilities to urban local bodies.

   •   These amendments decentralized governance and promoted grassroots democracy.

1.4.3 Judicial Review and Amendments

• Basic Structure Doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati Case)

   •   The Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) case is the most significant
       constitutional decision in Indian legal history.

   •   Facts:

          o     Swami Kesavananda Bharati challenged the Kerala land reform laws and the
                validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments.

   •   Judgment:

          o     The Supreme Court ruled that Parliament has wide powers to amend the
                Constitution under Article 368.

          o     However, it cannot alter or destroy the “basic structure” of the Constitution.

   •   Core elements of the Basic Structure include:

          o     Supremacy of the Constitution

          o     Republican and democratic form of government

          o     Secularism

          o     Separation of powers

          o     Federalism

          o     Unity and integrity of the nation

          o     Judicial review

          o     Free and fair elections

           o   Rule of law

           o   Harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

   •   The doctrine became a constitutional safeguard, preventing authoritarian
       amendments.

• Limits to Parliamentary Power

   •   The Basic Structure Doctrine places implied limitations on the amending power of
       Parliament.

   •   The Supreme Court has reaffirmed this in multiple cases:

Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975):

           o   Amendment to place election of Prime Minister beyond judicial review was
               struck down as unconstitutional.

Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980):

           o   Struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment that gave unlimited power to
               Parliament to amend the Constitution.

           o   Reaffirmed that limited government is part of the basic structure.

I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007):

           o   Held that laws inserted in the 9th Schedule after 1973 are also subject to
               judicial review if they violate basic structure.

   •   These judgments reinforce that:

           o   The amending power is not absolute.

           o   The Supreme Court is the final interpreter of the Constitution.

           o   Amendments that violate democracy, federalism, secularism, or judicial
               independence are unconstitutional.

1.5 Summary

Module 1 introduces the foundational concepts and historical evolution of the Indian
Constitution. It begins by exploring the colonial administrative legacy and the impact of British
legislations such as the Regulating Act of 1773 and the Government of India Acts of 1858,
1919, and 1935. These legal frameworks laid the groundwork for centralised governance and
codified laws, which significantly influenced post-independence constitutional design. The
module further examines the role of the Indian freedom struggle in shaping constitutional
aspirations, particularly through instruments like the Nehru Report, the Simon Commission
opposition, and the Round Table Conferences, all of which contributed to the demand for a

Constituent Assembly. The formal establishment of the Constituent Assembly, guided by the
Cabinet Mission Plan, marks a turning point in the constitutional journey. The Objectives
Resolution, presented by Jawaharlal Nehru, articulates the vision of an independent,
democratic, and inclusive India, and it deeply influenced the drafting process, especially the
Preamble. The debates within the Constituent Assembly involved extensive discussions on
federalism, minority rights, and governance structure, with significant contributions from
leaders such as Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, Sardar Patel, and Rajendra Prasad. The module concludes
by outlining the key features of the Constitution, including the Preamble, the thematic division
into Parts, and the functional detailing provided by the Schedules, all of which collectively
form the core architecture of India's constitutional democracy.

1.6 Keywords with Definitions

   1. Preamble: An introductory statement in the Constitution that outlines its guiding
      values and objectives such as justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity.

   2. Constituent Assembly: A body of elected representatives formed in 1946 to draft the
      Constitution of India.

   3. Objectives Resolution: A declaration presented by Nehru in 1946, setting forth the
      ideals that would guide the Indian Constitution.

   4. Schedules: Structured appendices in the Constitution that categorize administrative
      and legal details such as official languages, division of powers, and governance of tribal
      areas.

   5. Government of India Act, 1935: A key colonial legislation that introduced provincial
      autonomy and served as a blueprint for the Indian Constitution.

   6. Judicial Review: The power of courts to examine the constitutionality of legislative and
      executive actions.

   7. Federalism: A system of governance where power is divided between a central
      authority and constituent units like states.
